messages:
ana: Heads-up — saw a tenant spike get rate-limited in the fanout path this morning. ~2k events were dropped from the immediate billing stream, customer called it out.
liam: Oof. Do we have a reproducible trace? Where in the pipeline did the drop happen — the fanout worker? queue? rate-limiter? :thinking:
sara: Alert shows fanout worker emitting 429s to the downstream billing writer. It looked like we hit the per-tenant burst cap in the sharded fanout queue. Metric: fanout.rate_limit.rejections -> 2k
ana: Right. Question: do we want a short per-tenant grace buffer (ephemeral retention) to smooth bursts, or prefer stricter backpressure/requeue semantics? Tradeoffs: latency vs billing fidelity vs storage.
rob: Can we add a small in-memory spillover with TTL (e.g. 5m) per tenant, then drain to billing writer when capacity frees? That avoids permanent drops but costs memory + complexity for dedupe.
liam: Dedupe is the big gotcha. If we requeue, billing writer must be idempotent or we need a canonical event id. Do we already have event ids? yes — event.envelope.event_id exists.
sara: We do have event ids but late-arrival semantics matter. If we allow a 5m grace window we need to surface "late" vs "real-time" flags for downstream consumers (billing/alerts). Also metric explosion to track late-window replays.
ana: Example envelope we get:
```
{"tenant_id":"t-123","event_id":"evt-abc","ts":1765439000,"type":"token_usage","tokens":120}
```
rob: Implementation idea: if fanout worker sees rate-limit, write to ephemeral spill bucket (compact store) keyed by tenant + event_id with TTL. Schedule a background drain job that rate-limits itself to avoid thundering herd. If TTL expires without drain, emit tombstone indicating "dropped_due_to_capacity" so downstream accounting can mark gaps.
liam: That buys us durability and a signal for auditors. Alternative is to extend the per-tenant token bucket to allow short bursts by borrowing from global capacity, but that affects fairness.
sara: Cost estimate: ephemeral store at 5m TTL, worst-case tenant burst 50k events ~ average event size 1KB -> 50MB per tenant in worst case. Multiply by N tenants hits peak. Need quota guard.
rob: We can cap spill queue to N events per tenant (e.g., 50k) and then start emitting tombstones once cap hit. That keeps bounded storage and gives deterministic behavior.
ana: Operational hooks we need: 1) metric: spill.enqueue_count, spill.drain_count, spill.tombstone_emitted; 2) alert when spill.backlog > threshold; 3) dashboard showing late vs real-time billing splits.
liam: For correctness: billing writer must dedupe by event_id and accept a "replay" flag. Also preserve original ts to avoid double-charging windowed aggregations.
sara: Edge-case: what about multi-region? If tenant is multi-region and fanout is regional, must ensure spill drain is routed to same billing partition or partitioned coordinator for idempotency.
rob: Implementation sketch: use existing compact-store (sharded by tenant), write keys with TTL, drain via a controlled consumer group that throttles per-tenant. Tombstone entries are special events added to the billing stream: {event_id, tenant_id, reason:"spill_ttl_expired"}.
ana: Proposal: start with conservative config: TTL=5m, cap=50k events/tenant, drain window 0-2rps per-tenant depending on dedicated slots. Surface metrics + playbook. If pilot looks good expand.
liam: SGTM. Add RFC for config knobs + migration plan for regional tenants. I'll draft and assign owners.
sara: Note: need to update billing reconciler to treat tombstones as explicit gaps (do not generate synthetic charges) and surface to CS for manual review.
rob: I'll prototype the spill write/drain in a branch. Will reuse compact-store TTL API.
deploy-bot: deploy pipeline: no related deploys in last 24h for the fanout service.
ana: Action items: @liam write RFC (owner), @rob prototype, @ana add dashboards/alerts, @sara update reconciler behavior. Can we sync tomorrow 10am? :thumbsup:
liam: Yep. I'll create the RFC doc and link here.
ana: Thanks all — this should reduce customer-impacting drops without blowing up storage costs.
